question_text: If sin θ = a/(b + c), then show that cos θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).

steps.label: Square the given relation
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length. The sine is given this time, so cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ. Everything else follows the standard path.

recall.must_convey: That sin θ is squared and cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ formed.

steps.why: sin² + cos² = 1 works in either direction, which is why this question and the a = (b + c) cos θ question reach the SAME expression from opposite starting points.
steps.memory_tip: The sine is given this time, so cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ.

steps.label: Expand and use the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length. From here it is the standard route — expand, group, and apply the cosine rule.

recall.must_convey: That the expansion is grouped so b² + c² − a² can be replaced by 2bc cos A.

common_mistakes: Failing to group the three terms together.
steps.memory_tip: Expand (b + c)², then group so b² + c² − a² appears — that is 2bc cos A.

steps.label: Introduce the half angle
steps.margin_note: One of the two marks — the method mark for the whole derivation. 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2), the half-angle form that turns the bracket into a square.

accept: one plus cos A is two cos squared half A giving four b c cos squared half A

steps.why: A PLUS sign in front of cos A always means the cosine half-angle form. That single observation picks the right identity every time in this family.
common_mistakes: Reaching for the sine half-angle form.
steps.memory_tip: 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2), the same half of the pair as the a = (b+c)cos θ question.

steps.label: Take the square root
steps.margin_note: The last mark. The square root gives exactly the result the question states — which is worth noticing rather than doubting.

recall.must_convey: That the square root gives cos θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).

steps.why: Both twins land on the same right-hand side. That is not a coincidence — they start from the two halves of the same Pythagorean identity.
common_mistakes: Assuming the answer must differ from the twin and re-checking needlessly.
steps.memory_tip: The answer is identical to the cos θ question — worth noticing rather than doubting.

insider_note: Squaring leaves cos²θ, and the cosine rule turns (b+c)² − a² into 2bc(1 + cos A). The finish is the same as the a = (b+c)cos θ question; only the starting ratio differs.
